claims.claim: median optical properties from 46 Northern Hemisphere lakes: albedo 0.55 and attenuation 0.79 m⁻¹ for black ice, 0.60 and 4.35 m⁻¹ for white ice, 0.94 and 8.96 m⁻¹ for snow
claims.source_value: the six values are right, but they are the posterior medians (fixed component) of the ice-quality model, fitted to the 15 lakes that recorded black and white ice separately (626 daily observations), not to all 46 lakes; the 46-lake data set (722 observations, 31 lakes with total ice only) gives the single-layer total-ice model: αt 0.56, kt 1.75 m⁻¹, αs 0.90, ks 8.28 m⁻¹
claims.location: p. 1 (abstract); p. 5 of 12 (PDF p. 5), §2.2; p. 7 of 12 (PDF p. 7), §3; p. 4, Table 1 (model medians)
claims.quote: Ice quality data were recorded for 15 lakes (626 measurements)
claims.conditions: Bayesian mixed-effects Beer–Lambert fit (Stan); lakes 41–62° N; irradiance mostly PAR as photon flux (total shortwave in two Russian lakes); daily observations nearest noon; αs is the asymptotic snow albedo (thin snow corrected toward the ice's albedo with decay constant c = 0.019 m); k is the diffuse attenuation coefficient
claims.note: Say '15 of the 46 lakes (those with ice-quality data)'. 90 % bounds are wide for some: kb 0.24–1.46, kw 2.94–7.35, ks 7.35–10.54 m⁻¹ (Table 1). The units (m⁻¹) are confirmed in the full text, so the paper's caveat 'units confirmed only in a secondary summary' can go.

claims.claim: values varying widely between studies (and the units are m⁻¹)
claims.location: p. 3 of 12 (PDF p. 3), §2.1; p. 4, Table 1 (literature ranges); p. 6, Eq. 1
claims.quote: substantial variability across studies exists, especially in α, and in k for snow
claims.conditions: literature compilation (Figure 1): e.g. black-ice albedo 0.08–0.35 (n = 5), snow k 5–33.4 m⁻¹ (n = 10)
claims.note: The model's own ks (8.96) is about half the literature median (15.5); its αb (0.55) is far above the literature's (0.15), which the authors read as an effective season-averaged value fitted jointly with kb (p. 7).

claims.claim: layered, these give ~33 % transmission through 40 cm of snow-free black ice, 1.8 % under 10 cm of snow and 0.3 % under 30 cm
claims.location: p. 6 of 12 (PDF p. 6), Eqs. 1–2; p. 4, Table 1
claims.quote: where Eui is the under‐ice irradiance, Eai is the irradiance above the ice‐snow cover
claims.conditions: Eq. 1: Eui = (1 − α)·Eai·exp(−kb·hb − kw·hw − ks·hs), α the albedo of the uppermost layer
claims.note: Redone with the medians: 40 cm black ice 0.45·e^(−0.316) = 32.8 %; + 10 cm snow 0.06·e^(−1.212) = 1.79 % (1.85 % with the thin-snow albedo correction, Eq. 2, c = 0.019 m); + 30 cm snow 0.06·e^(−3.004) = 0.30 %. The model (src/w3/env3.js:388) ramps the snow albedo in linearly over 3 cm instead of Eq. 2's exponential with c = 0.019 m — a close stand-in.

claims.claim: light under ice is a layered Beer–Lambert transmission with Donini et al.'s median albedos and extinction coefficients
claims.quote: ks = 8.96 m− 1 for diffuse attenuation coefficients when ice quality data were considered
claims.note: The model's form (top-layer albedo, then each layer's exponential) is the paper's Eq. 1, and src/config.js:609 holds the six medians exactly (SNOW 0.94/8.96, WHITE 0.60/4.35, BLACK 0.55/0.79).

notes: Full text read (12 pp.). Other values the rewrite may want: total ice (single layer, 46 lakes) αt 0.56, kt 1.75 m⁻¹ (90 % 1.17–2.35); snow decay constant c = 0.019 m (literature 0.020); among-lake variation was small except for white ice (humic bog lakes Trout Bog and Crystal Bog had much higher kw, as cDOM is trapped in white ice), so a clear-water lake like Hot Brook may sit below the median kw. The authors stress snow and white ice dominate the attenuation and its uncertainty. Data and R scripts are public (Donini et al. 2025, cited in the Availability Statement).
